questions.question: A hawk's hooked beak, a turtle's hard shell and a cactus's sharp spines each help a living thing survive where it lives. What is a feature like this called?
questions.context: An adaptation is a feature, passed down from parents to young, that helps a living thing survive in its surroundings. An instinct is a behaviour an animal is born able to do, a learned skill comes from practice or being taught, and a habitat is the place where a living thing lives.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.13A has 5th graders analyze how body and plant parts help living things survive, and 'adaptation' is the word those units teach for such a part.

questions.question: Ducks, geese and many other water birds have webbed feet that push against the water like paddles. How does a duckling come to have webbed feet?
questions.answer: It inherits them from its parents
choices: It inherits them from its parents
Swimming stretches its toes into webs
It grows them because it wants to swim
Cold pond water makes its toes grow webs
questions.context: Webbed feet are passed down from parents to young, and a duckling's webs take shape while it is still growing inside the egg, before it has ever swum. No animal can grow an adaptation by wanting it or by using a body part; adaptations build up over many generations.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade adaptation units teach that adaptations are inherited, not chosen or gained in one lifetime, building on the inherited traits of NGSS 3-LS3-1.

questions.question: An animal has a thick layer of fat, called blubber, under its skin and a coat of dense fur on top. Where would these body coverings suit it best?
questions.context: Blubber is the thick fat of sea mammals such as seals and walruses, and it is thickest in those of icy polar seas, where it holds body heat in against the freezing water. Animals of snowy mountains, such as mountain goats, keep warm mainly with thick, woolly coats that trap air; blubber belongs to animals of the sea.
questions.grade_note: Matching body coverings to a habitat, such as thick fur for arctic cold, is a standard TEKS 5.13A activity.

questions.question: A sandy-brown lizard lies still on the desert sand. A hawk circling overhead looks straight down at it and never spots it. What kind of adaptation keeps the lizard safe?
questions.context: Camouflage is colouring that matches an animal's background, so a hunter's eyes pass right over it. Mimicry is looking like a different kind of animal, as a harmless hoverfly striped like a wasp does; warning colours are bright colours that tell hunters an animal is poisonous or stings; and moulting is shedding old skin, feathers or fur.
questions.grade_note: Camouflage is the colouring adaptation every 5th-grade adaptation unit teaches, as in TEKS 5.13A's earth-coloured horned lizard.

questions.question: A bird has a short, thick, cone-shaped beak, wide at the base and pointed at the tip. What job is a beak like this best built for?
questions.context: Seed-eating birds such as finches have stout, cone-shaped beaks that crush seeds. A long, thin beak reaches nectar deep in a flower, a sharp hooked beak tears meat, and a long, slender bill probes mud for small animals.
questions.grade_note: Matching beak shapes to foods is the classic bird-beak lesson of grades 3 to 5 and a TEKS 5.13A example of structure and function.

questions.question: A museum shows the skull of an animal with wide, flat back teeth, ridged for grinding, and no long, pointed teeth at the front. What did this animal mostly eat?
questions.context: Plant-eaters such as horses have broad, flat back teeth, ridged for grinding tough grass and leaves. Hunters such as foxes, which catch rabbits and mice, and shrews, which catch beetles and worms, have sharp, pointed teeth; bears, which eat berries and fish, have flat back teeth but long, pointed teeth at the front as well.
questions.grade_note: Elementary skull lessons for grades 3 to 5 teach students to tell plant-eaters from meat-eaters by the shape of their teeth.

questions.question: A cactus can go for months in the desert without a drop of rain, and it swells up when rain finally comes. Where does a cactus store most of its water?
questions.context: A cactus's thick, fleshy green body is its stem, which works as its water tank, and its pleats let it swell after rain and shrink in dry months. Most cacti have no ordinary leaves: their spines are leaves of a special kind that guard the plant from animals, and their shallow roots spread wide to soak up rain quickly.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.13A materials give the cactus's thick, water-storing stem and its spines as the model plant adaptations for a desert.

questions.question: Many trees in lands with snowy winters drop their leaves in autumn and grow new ones in spring. How does dropping the leaves help these trees?
questions.answer: They save water in the frozen months
choices: They save water in the frozen months
They make room for spring's new leaves
They stop the bark from cracking in frost
They help the roots drink melting snow
questions.context: Leaves let water escape into the air, and in winter the frozen ground gives the roots little water to replace it, so a bare tree loses far less. Next spring's leaves already wait in buds that formed in late summer, bare trunks can still split open in a hard frost, and with no leaves to pull water up, the roots drink less, not more.
questions.grade_note: Trees that shed their leaves for winter are one of the plant adaptations 5th-grade units teach beside the cactus and deep desert roots.

dd7c6fd7bb.why: Judge (medium): 'a part of a living thing' ruled out 'A habitat', and 'A life cycle' was no live lure. The stem drops the phrase, and 'A learned skill' (F22) replaces 'A life cycle': the 5th grader's real confusion of an adaptation with something learned in one life. Key unchanged.

7bdcbe11d7.why: Fact-check (precision note): not every water bird is web-footed (grebes and coots have lobed toes), so the stem now says 'many other water birds'. Choices, key and context unchanged.

a0fd1358f8.why: Judge (medium): the key was the only cold place, so dense fur alone gave it away and blubber was never tested. 'Snowy mountain peaks' replaces 'Dry grasslands': fur suits a mountain's cold too, but blubber belongs to sea mammals and is thickest in polar ones (F8, F23), as the context now says. Stem and key unchanged.

cf53b403b1.why: Judge (high): the stem ruled out 'Hibernation' and 'Migration' (the lizard lies still in plain view). They are replaced with 'Mimicry' and 'Moulting', colouring and skin words the stem cannot rule out (F24, F25), and the context defines both. Stem and key unchanged; this unit keeps the desert lizard and hawk, and ecosystems-living-and-nonliving moved its abiotic question to a pond.

e7b03bbb46.why: Fact-check (error): the context made sharp, pointed teeth a rule for every animal-eater, but ant- and termite-eaters have few or none. 'Beetles and ants' becomes 'Beetles and worms', and the context names real hunters (foxes, shrews, F27) instead of a rule. Judge (medium): the key was the only plant diet; 'Berries and fish', a bear's mixed diet (F26), replaces 'Fish and frogs', so the missing long front teeth now decide. Stem and key unchanged.

020c21c540.why: Judge (medium): 'In its flowers' was dead, and the real confusion (a cactus's fleshy body taken for leaves) was missing. 'In its leaves' replaces it, and the context says the fleshy body is the stem and the spines are its leaves (F16). Stem and key unchanged.

a92137039d.why: Judge (medium): the question could be answered from roots-stems-leaves-and-flowers' fact that roots take in water (the stem said desert), and 'Warmth deep in the ground' was no real lure. It now asks the contrast only this unit teaches, shallow roots against a deep one (F17, F18): both kinds take in water, so the old fact no longer decides it, and 'Dew that forms on the sand' (F28) replaces the warmth choice. Key unchanged.

749ce02e50.why: Judge (high): every wrong choice claimed an absurd gain (more food, more light, more growth with no leaves). The new lures sound like real winter reasons and are each sourced as wrong: next spring's leaves already wait in buds formed in late summer (F29), bare deciduous trees still get frost cracks (F30), and leaves are what pull water up from the roots (F31). The closer drops 'in winter', so no clause rules the spring lure out. Key unchanged.

dropped.question: Desert plants grow roots of two kinds. Some plants spread shallow roots wide, just under the ground; others send one root straight down many metres. What can the deep root reach that the shallow ones cannot?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: Stem tell, and the overlap is not cleared. The stem puts the shallow roots 'just under the ground' and asks what the deep root reaches 'that the shallow ones cannot'. That rules out both surface choices (rain soon after it falls, dew on the sand) by the stem's own logic. The one remaining lure, 'Food stored deep in the soil', falls to roots-stems-leaves-and-flowers' keyed fact (roots take in water, not food, with the same 'food from the soil' lure). So the old fact plus 'deep' still decides it, as the judge warned. The facts themselves are true.
